1:
Gill opens with the arithmetic. Ahaziah's two years were not complete: he began in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat and died towards the close of the eighteenth, so Jehoram succeeded him then and reigned twelve years. Ellicott adds that "began to reign" is in the Hebrew simply "reigned", and takes the formula of verse 2 to mean that Jehoram maintained the illicit worship of the bullock at Beth-el. Clarke puts it more concretely: he abolished the worship of Baal but continued that of the calves at Dan and Beth-el.

The interesting question is what Jehoram actually did to the image, and a textual crux decides a moral verdict. Ellicott notes that the word rendered "image" is a pillar, that the Greek, the Vulgate and the Arabic read pillars in the plural on a different pointing, and that the Greek adds at the end "and brake them in pieces". He judges that addition original, reasoning that Ahab would be likely to set up more than one pillar to Baal. Henry, reading the shorter text, builds his heaviest charge on precisely what the Greek supplies: Jehoram only put the image away, he did not break it in pieces as he ought to have done, but laid it aside for the present, not knowing but he might have occasion for it another time. On Ellicott's reading that charge cannot stand. Ellicott has his own account of why the worship survived, since Jezebel lived throughout the reign and the pillar must afterwards have been restored, probably by her influence; Henry reaches the same fact by another route, observing that Jezebel was content, for reasons of state, to worship her Baal in private.

Henry's indictment has three heads and the other two are untouched by the textual question. The reform was partial in its reach: Jehoram put away the image, probably in compliment to Jehoshaphat, who would not otherwise have come into confederacy with him, but he did not destroy the worship of Baal among the people, and Jehu found it still prevalent long afterwards. It was well to reform his family, Henry says, but it was not enough; he ought to have used his power for the reforming of his kingdom. It was partial in its object too, since he adhered to the calves, and Henry's explanation of that is political: the calves were the state engine by which the division between the two tribes was supported. His conclusion is the sharpest sentence in the chapter, that those do not truly, nor acceptably, repent or reform, who only part with the sins that they lose by, but continue their affection to the sins that they get by.

Wesley arrives at the same judgment through the same political reading, calling the calves a wall of partition which all the kings of Israel kept up between their subjects and those of Judah, so that although Jehoram had a little religion he had not enough to over-rule this policy. Ellicott, characteristically, spends his note on verse 3 on the grammar instead, observing that the pronoun rendered "therefrom" is a collective feminine and pointing to the same construction elsewhere in the book.

Henry allows that the influence in the alliance may have run both ways: Jehoshaphat, though by his alliance with the house of Ahab he made his own family worse, perhaps did something towards making Ahab's better. The irony Henry will not let go is that Jehoram was one of the best of that family, and that the destruction of it came in his days and fell immediately upon him, because by then the measure of its iniquity was full.
4:
Why the revolt went unpunished for a whole reign is variously explained. Gill offers three possibilities: Ahaziah was pusillanimous in temper, or hindered by the sickness that attended him, or had too short a reign; Ellicott points to the accident, Delitzsch to the short reign. Henry allows no excuse: it was folly and pusillanimity and indifference to the public good, the more aggravated because the Moabite tribute was a very considerable branch of the revenue of the crown of Israel. He adds that the riches of kings then lay more in cattle than coin, and taxes were paid not so much in money as in the commodities of the country, an ease to the subject whether or not it advantaged the prince.

What "sheepmaster" means divides Clarke and Ellicott, who reach it through different languages. Clarke reports that the Greek could make nothing of the Hebrew word and simply kept it, while the Chaldee, Aquila and Symmachus all render it sheepmaster; he derives it from a root meaning to mark or brand, supposing Mesha had his flocks marked in a particular way to ascertain his property. Ellicott goes to Arabic, where the cognate names a kind of sheep of superior wool and its owner, and fills out the picture with the country itself, mountainous but well watered and rich in fertile valleys, the Arabian wilderness lying open to Moabite flocks.

Whether the tribute was crushing is a real dispute. Ellicott parses the phrase closely: "with the wool" is rather "in wool", an accusative of limitation, and since the word for lambs means lambs fatted for food the wool belongs only to the rams, so the annual payment was a hundred thousand fatted lambs and the fleeces of a hundred thousand rams. That was a heavy burden, he says, for a country no larger than the county of Huntingdon, and he points to Mesha's own monument, which complains of the oppression of Moab by Omri and Ahab. Delitzsch, having established that the tribute was yearly and not merely due at each accession, concludes the opposite, that it could not be exorbitant for a land so rich in pasture. Wesley makes the wealth itself the cause, since it enabled and emboldened Mesha to rebel against his sovereign.

Ellicott is not uniformly deferential to the Greek. Here it adds "in the revolt", implying this rebellion was distinct from the earlier one and the tribute an indemnity for it; Ellicott judges the addition probably a transcriber's, though two verses earlier he had taken another Greek plus as original. He also notices that Jehoshaphat's answer is word for word his answer to Ahab, and passes on the inference that this section came from the same hand as parts of 1 Kings.

On the alliance Henry is of two minds within a paragraph. He admires the magnanimity, that Jehoshaphat did not upbraid Israel with the old revolt from the house of David nor make return to allegiance an article of the treaty but treated it as a sister-kingdom, and moralises that those are no friends to their own peace who can never find in their hearts to forgive an old injury. Then he turns: Jehoshaphat had like to have paid dearly for joining with Ahab, joined with his son anyway, and there is nothing got by being yoked with unbelievers. Wesley supplies the political motive Henry leaves out, that revolters had to be chastised lest the example pass into Jehoshaphat's own dominions and encourage the Edomites, as in fact they did revolt under his son. On the southern route they converge: Clarke and Henry both note that it brought in the king of Edom, who being tributary was obliged to come, and Ellicott adds that Moab's strongest defences lay on the north, that the northern march risked attack from the Syrians, and that the Moabites would be less on their guard southward.
9:
Delitzsch and Ellicott put the army in the same ravine. Delitzsch notes that the usual route into Moab, taken by the Crusaders and by later travellers, runs round the Dead Sea and up the Wady ed Deraah to Kerak, and that the allies went instead by the Wady el Kurahy, called the Wady el Ahsy farther up in the mountains, a ravine through which Burckhardt passed with the greatest difficulty. Ellicott names the same deep rocky glen between Moab and Edom and supplies the reason the plan failed: water is usually found there even in the dry season, and this time there was none.

Why the march took seven days is answered three ways. Clarke thinks it was simply ill planned. Ellicott suspects they lost their way among the mountains of Seir, and adds that they would in any case be greatly delayed by the cattle it was necessary to take for subsistence. Wesley makes it deliberate: the army was great and moved slowly, and they fetched a greater compass than usual for some advantage they expected by it. Ellicott reads the verse more exactly than the Authorised Version allows: the stopping is wrong, and the sense is that there was no water for the army or for the cattle which followed the kings, meaning the herds and flocks kept for its maintenance. He also observes that the distress began only after the Edomite contingent joined.

Jehoram's cry that the Lord has called three kings together to deliver them into the hand of Moab is taken at face value by one and as evasion by two. Clarke reads it as sound theology: this is a divine judgment, and God has judicially blinded them. Gill points out that Jehoram was the principal who drew the others in, yet throws it on the Lord and his providence. Henry is blunter: it was he that called these kings together, yet he charges it upon Providence and reflects upon that as unkind, so the foolishness of man perverteth his way and his heart fretteth against the Lord. Delitzsch takes Elisha's coming rebuke as meant to humble a king already bowed down by trouble and to produce some salutary fruit of repentance.

Jehoshaphat comes off better, though not without reproach. Gill and Wesley both note that the question should have been asked before the expedition began, Wesley adding that he now suffers for it, his affliction bringing him to the remembrance of his former sin and present duty; Henry generalises that good men are sometimes remiss and neglect their duty till necessity and affliction drive them to it. Ellicott observes that the same question stands at the same point in the Ahab narrative, down to a Hebrew peculiarity he reads as a mark of the same hand.

That Elisha was already in the camp surprises them all. Ellicott holds he must have followed of his own accord, or rather under a divine impulse, that in the hour of trial he might point Jehoram to the only true God; Wesley says the same and draws the lesson that God provides for those who provide not for themselves. Ellicott and Henry agree that the servant who knew of him was likely a friend of the prophets, like Obadiah. On the phrase about pouring water Ellicott explains the custom of a servant pouring from a ewer over his master's hands, while Wesley adds that the office was the more necessary among the Israelites because of the frequent washings their law required. Henry draws the moral that he who would be great must learn to minister. Why three kings should walk down to a prophet's tent is again answered three ways. Henry makes it esteem in Jehoshaphat and mere straits in the others; Ellicott passes on the judgment that they were humbled by misfortune; Wesley makes it calculation, the honour being meant to engage his utmost assistance.
13:
Elisha's rebuke is divided between the parents in two ways. Ellicott takes "the prophets of thy father" to cover both the Baal prophets and the false prophets of the Lord, reading the sarcasm as evidence that the former had not been wholly rooted out. Wesley splits it by cult instead: to the calves which Jehoram worships after his father's example, and the Baals which his mother yet worships by his permission. Clarke notes a textual curiosity: the Chaldee and the Arabic both expand Jehoram's "Nay" into a plea for mercy, and though some such words were likely spoken, only these versions add them.

The minstrel draws the fullest comment, and two reach for the same classical parallel. Both cite Cicero's report that the Pythagoreans were accustomed to calm their minds by singing and playing on the harp, Ellicott adding that the incident is a striking mark of the historical truth of the narrative. They differ on what was troubling Elisha. Ellicott and Delitzsch keep to the sight of Jehoram, Delitzsch describing the music as collecting the mind from the impressions of the outer world to be absorbed in the intuition of divine things. Clarke reports that the rabbins and many Christians add the affair of the young men at Beth-el. Gill identifies the player, on Procopius Gazaeus' authority, as one of the Levites accustomed to the spiritual melody of David, and passes on the suggestion that the mode called for was the gravest and saddest sort. Wesley alone makes the music do more than calm, holding that Elisha was thereby excited to more fervent prayer, and takes the hand of the Lord for the spirit of prophecy, so named to mark that it was no virtue inherent in him.

Why dig the ditches is answered three ways. Clarke makes the digging part of the stratagem, a dry river channel widened into canals so that the reflection of the sun's rays from the water might confound the Moabites. Ellicott is hydrological: the pits, literally pits upon pits, were to gather water that would otherwise run away in the bed of the torrent. Henry makes it a test of faith and obedience: those who expect God's blessings must prepare room for them and dig the pools for the rain to fill.

The order to fell the trees collides with the law, and each escapes differently. Clarke denies that fruit trees are meant, since felling them was positively against the law. Gill offers three harmonisations: the law may respect only besieged cities, or only Canaanitish cities, or may have been dispensed with for this time only. Ellicott dissolves the conflict grammatically: the verbs are continuative and foretell the course of the war rather than commanding it, and the law covered territory Israel was to occupy, not an enemy's country. Wesley justifies the severity, the Moabites being perfidious and implacable enemies now in rebellion.

On the water Clarke and Ellicott divide over what kind of event this was. Clarke calls the supply altogether miraculous, since there was neither wind nor rain nor any other natural means by which it could be supplied. Ellicott suggests a sudden storm on the mountains of Seir, at some distance from the camp, whose water found its natural outlet in the dry wady, and defends this against the objection that it is superfluous where a miracle is intended: there are different kinds of miracle, and here it lies in the prophet's prediction and in the coincidence of the natural phenomena with the need. The others make the timing the point. Delitzsch takes the hour of the morning sacrifice as a sign that God was restoring his favour on account of the offering in his temple; Wesley goes further, reading it as a public testimony from heaven for the Jews and against the Israelites, which Ellicott also entertains as an indirect hit at the northern kingdom.
21:
The Moabites' mistake is explained, not merely reported. Clarke thinks it may have been an optical deception, adding that he has seen the like where there was no reason to suspect supernatural agency, and that the Moabites, never having seen that valley full of water, did not suspect their eyes. Ellicott notes that the sun rose behind the Moabites, and suggests the red earth of the locality may have deepened the colour. Both find the inference reasonable: confederates of different races had fallen out before, as Midianites and Philistines had, and Ellicott adds that the old enmity of Edom towards Israel and the jealousies between Israel and Judah made such a result very likely. Henry traces the self-deception step by step: what we wish we readily believe, and none are so effectually deceived as those that deceive themselves.

Ellicott's work on the pursuit is textual. He reads the clause about Kir-haraseth as limiting what precedes: the cities they kept overthrowing until her stones were left in Kir-haraseth, so the destruction stopped at the walls of the chief stronghold, while in the other cities not one stone was left upon another. What the slingers did divides them. Ellicott has them shooting at the men on the walls with deadly effect, Wesley has them slinging great stones to break the walls down, and Clarke gives both, the slingers clearing the wall while the besieging army sapped the foundations. On the sortie Clarke and Delitzsch agree the Edomite quarter looked weakest; Ellicott allows that but adds a second possibility, that Mesha hoped these unwilling allies of Israel would let him escape through their ranks.

Whose son was offered was once disputed, and Gill's whole note settles it. Some made the victim the king of Edom's son, held hostage or seized in the sortie; Gill answers that the king of Edom, being but a deputy king himself, could have no son with a right to succeed him, and that sacrificing such a hostage would have provoked the kings to press the siege rather than raise it. Clarke reports a rabbinic story in which Mesha's servants trace Israel's miracles to the merit of Abraham offering his only son, and the king replies that he too has an only son; Clarke also records, and rejects as not very solid, the suggestion that the offering was made not upon the wall but to the sun, the Hebrew words differing by a letter. Delitzsch and Ellicott agree the sacrifice was to Chemosh and not to the God of Israel, Ellicott citing Mesha's own inscription that Chemosh was angry with his land, and noting that the Hebrews themselves were prone to the same rites in dark times.

The last clause is the hardest in the chapter, and the readings are irreconcilable. Clarke offers two: the Lord was displeased with them for driving things to such an extremity, or the surrounding nations held them in abomination for it and they were themselves so terrified that they raised the siege. Henry takes the second and draws a rule: tender and generous spirits will not do what is just if it will drive any man distracted, and it is well not to urge the worst of men to extremities. Ellicott reads the phrase as always denoting a visitation of divine wrath, sees its manifestation in a successful sortie by a garrison newly emboldened, and then asks why such wrath should fall upon the involuntary cause rather than the voluntary agents. If the wrath meant is the Lord's, he says, we cannot tell. His own answer is that the expiation attained its object and the wrath of Chemosh fell upon the Hebrew alliance, since belief in the supremacy of Jehovah did not hinder ancient Israel from admitting the real existence and potency of foreign deities, a conception he reads as a token of the antiquity of the record.
